mcqs.q: Pathologic calcification is the abnormal deposition of:
opts: Calcium salts in tissues where bone/enamel does not normally form
mcqs.explain: Pathologic (heterotopic) calcification is deposition of calcium salts in soft tissues that do not normally mineralise.

mcqs.q: The two types of pathologic calcification are:
mcqs.explain: Pathologic calcification is classified as dystrophic (in damaged tissue) and metastatic (in normal tissue with hypercalcaemia).

mcqs.q: Dystrophic calcification occurs in:
opts: Dead or damaged tissue, with NORMAL serum calcium
Normal living tissue with high calcium
mcqs.explain: Dystrophic calcification deposits in dead/damaged tissue while the serum calcium level is normal.

mcqs.q: Metastatic calcification occurs in:
opts: Only dead tissue with normal calcium
mcqs.explain: Metastatic calcification affects normal tissue and is driven by raised serum calcium (hypercalcaemia).

mcqs.q: Which condition would lead to METASTATIC calcification?
mcqs.explain: Any cause of hypercalcaemia (e.g. hyperparathyroidism) leads to metastatic calcification; atheroma and TB cause dystrophic calcification.

mcqs.q: A classic site of DYSTROPHIC calcification is:
opts: An atheromatous plaque or a tuberculous focus
mcqs.explain: Dystrophic calcification develops in advanced atheroma, ageing/damaged heart valves and tuberculous (necrotic) foci — damaged tissue with normal serum calcium.

mcqs.q: Intracellular accumulations occur due to all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Increased blood flow to the cell
Lack of the enzyme needed to remove it
mcqs.explain: Accumulations result from overproduction, inadequate metabolism, or lack of the enzyme to remove a substance — not from increased blood flow.

mcqs.q: Fatty change (steatosis) is the abnormal accumulation of:
mcqs.explain: Fatty change (steatosis) is abnormal accumulation of triglycerides within parenchymal cells, most often the liver.

mcqs.q: Fatty change is MOST often seen in the:
mcqs.explain: Fatty change occurs most often in the liver (also heart, skeletal muscle, kidney).

mcqs.q: Which is a cause of fatty liver?
mcqs.explain: Fatty liver follows excess fat (obesity, diabetes) or liver cell damage (alcohol, toxins, steroids, starvation, protein malnutrition).

mcqs.q: On microscopy, fatty change in hepatocytes shows:
opts: Lipid vacuoles that push the nucleus to the periphery
mcqs.explain: Lipid vacuoles accumulate in the cytoplasm and displace the nucleus to the periphery, giving an 'empty cell' appearance.

mcqs.q: Carbon (anthracosis) is an example of which pigment type?
mcqs.explain: Carbon is an exogenous pigment inhaled as an air pollutant; it is taken up by alveolar macrophages (anthracosis).

mcqs.q: After inhalation, carbon pigment is taken up by:
mcqs.explain: Inhaled carbon is taken up by alveolar macrophages, which are coughed out or settle in the lung interstitium.

mcqs.q: Tattoo pigment is an example of:
opts: Localized exogenous pigmentation taken up by dermal macrophages
mcqs.explain: Tattooing is a localized exogenous skin pigmentation; the dye is taken up by dermal macrophages and persists indefinitely.

mcqs.q: Lipofuscin is best described as:
opts: A brown 'wear-and-tear' pigment of ageing/atrophy in lysosomes
mcqs.explain: Lipofuscin (lipo = fat, fuscin = brown) is the brown-yellow 'wear-and-tear' intra-lysosomal pigment that accumulates with age/atrophy.

mcqs.q: Lipofuscin is commonly seen in the:
mcqs.explain: Lipofuscin accumulates in the heart, hepatocytes and neurons as residual bodies with ageing.

mcqs.q: Decreased melanin pigmentation is characteristic of:
mcqs.explain: Melanin is a brown-black endogenous pigment; it is decreased in vitiligo and increased in some lesions/melanoma.

mcqs.q: Haemosiderin is:
mcqs.explain: Haemosiderin is a golden-brown iron-storage pigment; excess deposition is termed haemosiderosis.

mcqs.q: Which is an ENDOGENOUS pigment?
mcqs.explain: Endogenous pigments (made in the body) include lipofuscin, melanin and haemosiderin; carbon and tattoo dye are exogenous.

mcqs.q: In dystrophic calcification, the serum calcium level is:
mcqs.explain: Dystrophic calcification occurs with a NORMAL serum calcium level (the tissue is damaged); metastatic calcification needs hypercalcaemia.

mcqs.q: Metastatic calcification commonly deposits in:
opts: Normal tissues such as gastric mucosa, kidney and lungs
mcqs.explain: Because it is driven by hypercalcaemia, metastatic calcification deposits in normal tissues — commonly gastric mucosa, kidney and lungs.

mcqs.q: An accumulation caused by 'lack of the enzyme to remove a substance' is an example of accumulation due to:
mcqs.explain: A missing or deficient enzyme prevents removal of a substance, leading to its intracellular accumulation (e.g. storage diseases).

saqs.a: Dystrophic: in dead/damaged tissue, NORMAL serum calcium (e.g. atheroma, TB). Metastatic: in normal tissue, HIGH serum calcium (hypercalcaemia, e.g. hyperparathyroidism).

saqs.q: List the three mechanisms of intracellular accumulation.
saqs.a: Overproduction of a substance, inadequate metabolism, and lack of the enzyme needed to remove it.

saqs.q: Define fatty change and give its microscopic appearance.
saqs.a: Abnormal accumulation of triglycerides in parenchymal cells (mostly liver). Microscopy: lipid vacuoles push the nucleus to the periphery (empty-cell look).
Excess fat (obesity, diabetes) or liver damage (alcohol, toxins, steroids, starvation, protein malnutrition).

saqs.q: Give two exogenous pigments and how they enter the body.
saqs.a: Carbon (inhaled → alveolar macrophages → anthracosis) and tattoo dye (injected → dermal macrophages, permanent).

saqs.q: What is lipofuscin and where is it found?
saqs.a: A brown 'wear-and-tear' intra-lysosomal pigment of ageing/atrophy, found in the heart, liver and neurons.
